A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OU@ε, Prototypical Relearning Attack and Spotter work. All 15 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v3, including figures, equations, tables and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR experiments, hyperparameter and attack ablations, and transformer-model evaluations in Tables 1–5.

after.justification: V3 retains original experiments and adds Tiny-ImageNet, CASIA-WebFace, repeated-attack, sequential-unlearning and forget-ratio results.

M1.justification: Spotter's three losses, weighted objective and prototype-head interpolation remain unchanged. Algorithm 1's corrected cosine normalization matches the formula already present in v1. The newly documented CLS-token extraction concerns transformer experiments already reported in v1; it does not establish a new architecture or procedure.

E1.justification: V3 adds Tiny-ImageNet classification and CASIA-WebFace identity unlearning beyond the retained CIFAR coverage (Appendix D). It also introduces sequential deletion requests, changing the task from a single unlearning operation to maintaining behavior across successive requests (Appendix G).

E2.justification: The nine standalone baselines remain, but the CIFAR comparison removes Spotter combinations with Random Label, NegGrad, Boundary Shrink, Boundary Expand, Learn to Unlearn and Fisher. Only SalUn, DELETE and UNSC combinations remain in v3 Table 2. The Gaussian comparison also removes retraining and all nine combined methods, substantially narrowing comparison coverage.

E3.justification: V3 adds a λ2=0.1 configuration, ten sequential rounds with one forgotten class per round, 30%/50% forgetting settings, and an attack-budget sweep using 1, 5, 10 and 100 samples. The retained CIFAR splits, three-step PGD evaluation at ε=0.03 and primary five-sample attack remain unchanged. Newly stated PGD implementation details do not establish changes to those existing experiments.

E4.justification: V3 adds Grad-CAM analysis of identity cues before and after attack, repeated randomized attacks addressing SalUn's residual micro-cluster concern, and robustness tests for sequential and large-fraction unlearning (Figure 4; Appendices F–H). Existing ε, λ and α analyses remain, while Gaussian robustness comparisons are reduced.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-experiment averaging for the main comparison. V3 Appendix F additionally reports 500 attack repetitions for each sample budget and summarizes the highest observed Proto-Accf. This introduces a limited worst-observed reporting practice without adding confidence intervals or general uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New results cover additional datasets, sequential deletion, larger forget fractions and attack stress tests. The added λ2=0.1 row reports Proto-Accf of 62.12%/88.32% on CIFAR-10/100; v1's Spotter results remain as λ2=1. Six combined pipelines, Gaussian rows and retrained-model OU values are removed. UNSC's CIFAR-10 Accr changes from 99.99% to 99.98% in Table 1. Added settings do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Equation 1 replaces v1's margin-buffer neighborhood, constrained by |gc|≤β, with a perturbation-generator definition allowing local ε-ball or boundary-crossing perturbations. V1's formal MU definition and exact/approximate distinction are also removed. The divergence metric and prototype derivations remain, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The three central contributions remain. V3 explicitly scopes them to class-level unlearning and replaces the abstract's specific CIFAR performance statement with a state-of-the-art claim spanning CIFAR, Tiny-ImageNet and CASIA-WebFace. This refines applicability and performance claims without redefining the central contribution.

C2.justification: V3 develops a white-box, few-sample threat interpretation for identity services, qualifies the SalUn micro-cluster concern through random sampling assumptions, and interprets Grad-CAM and sequential-deletion evidence. It removes v1's explicit explanation that successful attacks on retrained models reflect generalization rather than leftover memory. These materially change applicability boundaries and interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 specifies the PGD infinity norm, random start and 0.01 step size, explicitly states λ1=0.7, documents transformer CLS features, and corrects cosine normalization in the pseudocode. It omits v1's code-access link and explicit rule reusing baseline α for combined methods. Hardware and software disclosures remain unchanged; repository availability cannot be inferred from the missing link.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially to evaluation critiques, limitations of retraining as a reference, federated unlearning, poisoning, inversion and newer relearning defenses. Added works include Cooper et al., Hayes et al., Thaker et al. and Yuan et al. The positioning shifts from attacks never being addressed in vision to class-centric vision threats remaining underexplored.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, results discussion and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The standalone preliminaries section disappears, setup material moves into the metric section, results gain thematic subsections, and the α appendix is incorporated into attack details. An Impact Statement replaces the previous acknowledgments section.

P2.justification: V3 adopts a two-column main layout and splits the main comparison into standalone and combined-method tables with before-to-after cells. It adds Grad-CAM and four new experimental tables. Figure 1 replaces the retrained-model panel with SalUn; the existing ε plots are reordered and reformatted as Figure 5, retaining their curves.

improvement.justification: V3 strengthens empirical relevance through new domains, sequential deletions and 500-trial attack stress tests beyond v1's CIFAR evaluation. The net gain is limited by removed compatibility comparisons and the code pointer. New-domain results lack held-out test accuracy, and Table 10's 50% forgetting attack lowers retained accuracy from 99.94% to 97.29%, exceeding the stated one-point limit without explanation.
